title: Solitude and Leadership
author: William Deresiewicz
quote: Solitude is the very essence of leadership.
summary: A lecture to first-year West Point cadets arguing that leaders must be able to think for themselves, and that the institutions training them mostly produce skilled box-tickers. His remedy is solitude in three forms: undistracted concentration, reading old books, and deep one-to-one conversation, so you know what you believe before the hard decisions arrive.

title: Treat your to-read pile like a river, not a bucket
author: Oliver Burkeman
quote: There are simply too many rocks to fit in the jar.
summary: Your reading pile is not a failure of filtering; it is a surplus of things you genuinely want to read. Burkeman says the same “too many needles” logic runs through life: you cannot fit everything in, so choose what matters most, and treat the pile as a stream you dip into rather than a bucket you must empty.

title: Three pages a day
author: Oliver Burkeman
quote: You just do the pages, and something else does the rest.
summary: Burkeman’s most durable self-help habit is Morning Pages: write by hand until three sides are full, with no aim beyond keeping the pen moving. He argues its value comes from loosening the part of you that wants to control outcomes, which makes it closer to a ritual or a meditation than a productivity trick.

title: Taming the Mammoth: Why You Should Stop Caring What Other People Think
author: Tim Urban
quote: An irrational and unproductive obsession with what other people think of us.
summary: Urban pictures a “Social Survival Mammoth” in your head, built for life in a tiny tribe, that makes you fear disapproval, while your “Authentic Voice” quietly knows what you actually want. He shows how Puppet Masters end up running people’s lives, and what it takes to shrink the mammoth and act on your own voice.

title: Good conversations have lots of doorknobs
author: Adam Mastroianni
quote: Conversations, like improv scenes, start to sink if they sit still.
summary: Drawing on improv, Mastroianni says good conversations are full of doorknobs: small hooks the other person can grab and turn into a new topic. Weak ones stall because nobody hands over anything to hold. He looks at the biases that stop us offering or noticing them, and suggests simply offering plenty.
